elements.text:
It's been a little slow this past, with my son visiting from school. I've implemented confirmations by the downloading protocols when under checkpoint/milestone, so that confirmations are written in parallel. Otherwise this adds about 10 minutes to the run.

I've also implemented a generalized determination of combined checkpoint/milestone (bypass) height by the organizer, which is then broadcasted to the validation and confirmation chasers. This allows them to track and switch modes at almost no cost.

However, the block_in protocol also requires this information, but as protocols are many and come and go constantly with channels, it's not possible to initialize the bypass height at startup as with the others. So I'm working on an efficient mechanism for this. One might assume that they could simply initialize active milestone height from the store at startup, but this presents two problems:

(1) the query is a cost (though very small), and (2) the organizer controls the candidate chain, to which milestones are relative. Checkpoints on the other hand are assured by header validation, so those are trivial. The issue then is how to ensure proper ordering of the milestone to the protocol. I implemented this as a relay, where the protocol requests it at startup and the organizer responds with the corresponding message. However the need to delay the protocol during this communication relay costs about 20 minutes over a full run. So still looking at it.

elements.text: The machine is old, so no AVX512 (which will cut the two Merkle roots per block in half) and no SHANI (which will cut most sha256 by 80%). SHANI is also not yet integrated. The Merkle computations are presently only around 0.75% of the run, but sha256 is about 10%. That's are the only material optimizations that remain in the checkpoint/milestone sync realm.

elements.text: I struggled with the above ordering issue, and another similar issue related to deconfirming in the case of an invalidated block under a valid header chain, and another related to block hash malleability. I ended up implementing a relatively simple concept between the check chaser (block download with block.check() context free validation) and the channel download protocol that fans out to provide concurrent download/check. Basically the problem was that there was no way to invoke code at the completion of a purge in the downloading as a consequence of a reorganization or disorganization (which I refer to as regression - where the chain moves backward before moving forward again). I added a new race class to manage this, which has almost no cost.

elements.text: The optimal node is maximal disorder, which implies some necessary level of order.  The chasers exist to impose this order, and in working with this model over the past few months its become apparent that it is ideally suited for imposing the minimal level of order required while not imposing unnecessary costs to achieve it. But in order to avoid the inevitable race conditions certain general implementation rules have become apparent. These conceptually reduce to ensuring ownership over the several different aspects of ordering, while preserving the ability to provide the minimal necessary order between them.

elements.text: This allows us to safely implement complex but reasonable/optimal things. For example, the data model requires that each tx be associated to its confirming block header. This must be implemented in order as it is relied upon when confirmability queries are executed. However, when under checkpoint/milestone (validation/confirmation bypass) these associations can be written for all blocks under bypass as they are downloaded (out of order). As there are 1 billion txs, this is a material optimization. About 10 minutes over a full 65 minute run (would otherwise be 75 minutes).

elements.text: But milestones (unlike checkpoints) are subject to reorganization by a stronger branch. So what to do when an unknown set of blocks are confirmed and all of the sudden some of them have to become unconfirmed. Computing the potential set isn't so hard, but there needs to be a point when no more are being written from before the reorg, and none are yet being written from after the reorg. And in the midst of this there is the possibility that some blocks are malleable and therefore cannot be bypassed for validation/confirmation, and may be invalid even under bypass, and therefore require a download reinitialization. Managing optimal concurrency is non-trivial to say the least. But by following some simple rules can be made safe.

elements.text:
Sync is now running at under an hour on my 2Gbps Internet, and I've done a few tests of unoptimized concurrent validation, which completes in 3 hours. So I've spent the past few days on confirmation queries.

Download concurrency is limited by bandwidth - with no block ordering required. Validation concurrency is limited by CPU threads, and requires contiguous blocks but can validate any number concurrently. Confirmation is pure query, limited by disk speed (or exclusively RAM there is enough to hold the store), and can confirm blocks only one at a time in order - however transactions/inputs can be concurrently processed within each block.

text:
Sync is now running at under an hour on my 2Gbps Internet, and I've done a few tests of unoptimized concurrent validation, which completes in 3 hours. So I've spent the past few days on confirmation queries.

Download concurrency is limited by bandwidth - with no block ordering required. Validation concurrency is limited by CPU threads, and requires contiguous blocks but can validate any number concurrently. Confirmation is pure query, limited by disk speed (or exclusively RAM there is enough to hold the store), and can confirm blocks only one at a time in order - however transactions/inputs can be concurrently processed within each block.

elements.text: Starting at block 840,000 I ran some performance numbers on confirmation. Most of the confirmation cost, like 99.5% is determining confirmability. Updating state is trivial in comparison. On a cold store confirmation queries were averaging about 1-2 seconds per block. This gave me an opportunity to run the performance tools on intense querying for the first time. I was able to identify several areas where denormalization would produce material benefits. After a couple days of tuning store primitives, such as the
iterator
and the
hashmap
and the
head
, as well as simple modifications to several queries, the confirmation rate has increased to 5 per second, or roughly 5-10x faster than previously.

text: Starting at block 840,000 I ran some performance numbers on confirmation. Most of the confirmation cost, like 99.5% is determining confirmability. Updating state is trivial in comparison. On a cold store confirmation queries were averaging about 1-2 seconds per block. This gave me an opportunity to run the performance tools on intense querying for the first time. I was able to identify several areas where denormalization would produce material benefits. After a couple days of tuning store primitives, such as the `iterator` and the `hashmap` and the `head` , as well as simple modifications to several queries, the confirmation rate has increased to 5 per second, or roughly 5-10x faster than previously.

elements.text: Generally this only affects the tail of the chain, like validation, above the milestone block. However for a full chain validation that's too slow. Keep in mind that the first 300k blocks or so are trivial. These numbers are for full blocks, about 5k txs each. So 1 billion txs (at current heights) and 5,000 tx/block and 5 blocks/sec you get 25k txs/sec or 40,000 secs total (11.1 hours). If that can be divided in full by my 64 cores, it reduces to 10.4 minutes. However, disk speed is likely to be a limiting factor (CPU utilization is trivial). Moving on to that next.

Keep in mind that the first 300k blocks or so are trivial. These numbers are for full blocks, about 5k txs each. So 1 billion txs (at current heights) and 5,000 tx/block and 5 blocks/sec you get 25k txs/sec or 40,000 secs total (11.1 hours). If that can be divided in full by my 64 cores, it reduces to 10.4 minutes. However, disk speed is likely to be a limiting factor (CPU utilization is trivial). Moving on to that next.

elements.text:
Confirmation reads are sprawling, but there is very little data actually collected. The input and output tables, which contain the bulk of blockchain data aren't touched, since they are not hash tables (just blob tables referenced from others). So while there is a large amount of querying, data quickly populates RAM and disk activity slows significantly. It's dropped from 300MiB/s to 50MiB/s, with a disk capacity of 530MiB/s.

Over a span of the top 7,500 blocks, confirmation speed accelerated to 6.85 blocks/sec. Concurrency at full disk capacity (only about 1% of CPU is currently being used, on single thread) would put this at about 68 blocks/sec or 2,941 sec (49 minutes) for the full 1B txs). That assumes a good amount of RAM to limit page swaps. I had reached about 100GiB (with no swapping because I have 128GiB). But it's a low end SSD and in this example requires only 10 threads. It also assumes no concurrency with download and/or validation.

Also, for those testing out current master builds, you should be aware that all libbitcoin libs, but most importantly -system, are significantly impacted by compiler optimizations. In the visual studio builds optional settings are defaulted into the .props files for debug and release builds.

HOWEVER, the other builds require that you set these optimizations in the environment. This can be done as follows:
$ CFLAGS="-03" CXXFLAGS="-03" ./install.sh --build-boost --enable-ndebug --disable-shared --prefix=<path>

Because all hash functions are written in C++, you will get obscenely poor performance if you do not let the compiler fully optimize. With this setting the optimized code outperforms C implementations.

HOWEVER, the other builds require that you set these optimizations in the environment. This can be done as follows:

elements.text: There are also significant CPU-specific optimizations that you can set via the command line. These provide hash function vectorization at different levels. For example:
--enable-sse4
is the most basic and should be available on any supported CPU.
--enable-avx2
and
--enable-avx512

are also extremely common. I have been testing on a 7 year old machine that has sse4 and avx2 but not avx512. That allows 4 and and 8 lane vectorization, but not 16 lanes (avx512). If you set these then the build will enable them.

However, these are implemented such that portability is still enabled. This hurts performance, and so I have made a minor modification to one file locally...

elements.text: I've created an initial implementation for concurrent evaluation of confirmability. In libbitcoin validation and confirmability are distinct checks as they have distinct ordering constraints. Download is unordered by block, validation is partially ordered by block whereas confirmability is totally ordered by block. Yet, as with validation, confirmation is unordered by tx, and fuller blocks have around 4 thousand txs. This provides an opportunity to concurrently determine confirmability within a block, similarly to how we do with validation, which is concurrent by tx across multiple blocks.

text: I've created an initial implementation for concurrent evaluation of confirmability. In libbitcoin validation and confirmability are distinct checks as they have distinct ordering constraints. Download is unordered by block, validation is partially ordered by block whereas confirmability is totally ordered by block. Yet, as with validation, confirmation is unordered by tx, and fuller blocks have around 4 thousand txs. This provides an opportunity to concurrently determine confirmability within a block, similarly to how we do with validation, which is concurrent by tx across multiple blocks.

elements.text: I've run the concurrent-by-tx confirmability checks both after completing download and during download. Interestingly there is almost no increase in total download time, 5-10% at the most but this is within the typical range of download variation. 840,000 blocks are downloaded and archived in 69 minutes while at the same time the first 381,395 have been checked for confirmability. The total run completes in 2.5hrs, which is slightly faster than if all confirmation is performed at the completion of downloads. Notably, confirmation reads a huge amount of data (and writes very little). So on low memory machines it will suffer, and performing it during download is likely to produce terrible page churn.

elements.text: I've already optimized the related queries using the performance analyzer. There's not much left to work with in that regard, the confirmation process has been reduced almost entirely to pure disk reads, like 90% of it initially. So the process accelerates as the RAM starts to fill (from a cold start), and is eventually screaming (over 100 blocks per second) with no disk reads and 90% RAM full.

elements.text: I decided to take another look at modest memory/CPU configuration as it pertains to the confirmability query. On my max machine confirmability takes a total of 2.5 hrs running concurrently with 1 hr download (with no checkpoints/milestone). However on a 32GiB machine it blows up due to paging, taking at least 1 second per block on average. This is a huge cost that I don't presently have any mitigation for. As it's a consequence of disk read, concurrency provides only a modest improvement.

elements.text: It's likely that with more constrained RAM there is a paging cycle between these two tables, as they compete for RAM. The query performs on one block at a time (in order) and one tx at a time within the block (either in order or concurrently), with the spendable and spent subqueries within the tx query. This could be rotated to perform all spendable queries in the block before (or after) all spent, significantly reducing memory contention.

elements.text: I divided the per block confirmable queries into three natural sections, iterating over each in full before moving to the next. This reduces page swapping between tables. I then applied concurrency to each of the loops, using C++17 concurrency constructs. This results in at least a 300% improvement in confirmability for the baseline machine of 32GiB/10threads, averaging about 3 blocks per second, but this is still unacceptably slow. It appears that it has also modestly sped up the max machine, which previously completed in 2.5hrs, though I haven't evaluated that fully.

elements.text: With sufficient RAM to hold the indexes, and with the indexes fully loaded (as during a full sync), confirmability runs faster than concurrent download, and can run coincident with it. This implies no net cost, though its inherent ordering implies at least some small increase in total time over checkpoint/milestone sync.

elements.text: After a lot of performance analysis on the confirmation process, I've concluded that the current table design is too costly for lower RAM machines, unless maybe there is a very high speed SSD. Mine is pretty typical at about 500MB/sec r/w. With 256GiB RAM the entire thing runs in-memory, disk activity is trivial. Otherwise it is 100% (thrashing), even at 32GiB RAM, I didn't bother below that. So supporting full chain confirmation on low RAM machines (part of validation) will likely require additional indexation (or will take at least a day if not several).

text: After a lot of performance analysis on the confirmation process, I've concluded that the current table design is too costly for lower RAM machines, unless maybe there is a very high speed SSD. Mine is pretty typical at about 500MB/sec r/w. With 256GiB RAM the entire thing runs in-memory, disk activity is trivial. Otherwise it is 100% (thrashing), even at 32GiB RAM, I didn't bother below that. So supporting full chain confirmation on low RAM machines (part of validation) will likely require additional indexation (or will take at least a day if not several).

elements.text: On a 128GiB RAM machine with 64 cores, validating confirmability (without script validation) of all blocks requires about 90 minutes. Full chain validation (without confirmability) has independently tested out at 3 hours. That's before any caching or optimization work. I expect to be able to bring that down. Running these steps independently places a full chain download/validation/confirmation at under 6 hours, though on big machines these can be combined.

elements.text: So I'm moving on to optimizing concurrent validation. This will consist of maintaining downloaded/parsed blocks in memory (cache) for the validator, and prefetching prevouts. Both the block cache and disk can be used to populate prevouts for validation, which implies that the cache is not only block-ordered, but output-indexed. Protecting the cache and allowing it to operate on spare cycles ahead of the validator implies that it requires its own thread(s), so it's another chaser.

elements.text: There are several ways that costly loops can be parallelized, assuming that the design allows the concurrency. There are four loops that can be independently parallel, and setup synchronization can be accomplished via standard library execution policy on loops such as
std::all_of(...)

or via BOOST ASIO.

As std lib execution is only useful for simple loops, we use ASIO for network concurrency. I've learned in the past that the cost of using std lib execution policy can be very high. I tested it for simple two lane parallelization in RIPEMD and the result was horrific compared to just sequential execution. The only place we use it is in concurrency for scrypt hashing execution. In that case it provides a huge benefit with no ASIO complexities or dependency. The database queries are complex and costly, so I figured it was worth a look.

Turns out that using an ASIO thread pool, posting closures to the work queue, and tracking completion, absolutely crushes the much simpler loop vectorization.
std lib takes 133 mins to ASIO's 79 mins

.

I'm pretty sure that this type of performance difference would also impact C++20 co-routines. When I started on the network stack rewrite I looked at coroutines, but unlike the the rest of C++20, the reviews weren't good. A thread pool provide significant performance advantages, and these are now very visible.
